title: Italy's Fiscal Gamble: Debt, Energy Bills and the Limits of EU Flexibility
excerpt: Italy is navigating a simultaneous energy-price surge and a budget squeeze that threatens to push its 2027 deficit above the European Union's 3% ceiling. The Meloni government argues that defence commitments and a sharp energy shock justify exceptional fiscal room, but critics warn that debt near 138% of GDP leaves the country with dangerously little margin. The debate is as much about who pays now as about who pays later.
body:
A Budget Built on Borrowed Flexibility

Rome's latest fiscal projections place Italy's 2027 deficit at approximately 3.4% of GDP, above the EU's reference value of 3%, while public debt is expected to remain close to 138% of GDP. The Meloni government has framed the overshoot as a responsible compromise, noting that the deficit is projected to fall below 3% in 2026 before rising again the following year as defence spending and energy support measures take effect.

The government's growth assumptions, set at 1% in 2026 and 0.8% in 2027, have been assessed as broadly consistent by both the Parliamentary Budget Office and the Bank of Italy, lending some institutional credibility to the arithmetic underpinning the plan. Rome argues that Italy faces exceptional external pressures — rising NATO defence commitments and a renewed energy-price shock — that justify greater flexibility from Brussels, a case it intends to press directly with European institutions.

Critics, however, argue that the government is presenting a politically convenient version of fiscal discipline while postponing difficult structural choices. Rising debt-service costs and a deficit that is set to breach EU rules in 2027 reduce the space available for future tax cuts or welfare expansion, and opposition parties have questioned whether the prioritisation of defence and energy measures reflects genuine urgency or is partly designed to protect the governing coalition ahead of the next general election.

Energy Shock Drives Inflation to a Four-Year High

The energy dimension of Italy's budget dilemma is not abstract. Official data for September 2026 show annual consumer inflation accelerating to 4.2% from 3.3% the previous month, driven by regulated energy prices rising 25.9% year-on-year and non-regulated energy costs climbing 22.2%. By contrast, core inflation — which excludes energy and unprocessed food — stood at just 1.7%, a gap that points to a concentrated external shock rather than broad-based domestic overheating.

Those figures directly contradict claims, circulated by some government allies, that inflation is falling or already under control. The Bank of Italy expects overall inflation to average around 2.6% across 2026 before declining below 2% in subsequent years under its baseline scenario, suggesting the shock may prove temporary. But even if that forecast materialises, the damage to household purchasing power will not automatically reverse: prices that rise sharply do not return to their prior level simply because the rate of increase slows.

Trade unions have pressed for targeted relief, faster collective bargaining renewals and explicit wage-protection mechanisms. Their concern is grounded in official data: collectively agreed wages were expected to rise by approximately 2.5% in the absence of further renewals, a figure that already trailed underlying inflation and falls far short of the energy-driven headline rate. Small businesses and motorists have added their voices, particularly after the non-renewal of a diesel-tax reduction left transport costs exposed to the full force of the market price rise.

Brussels, Markets and the Politics of Who Pays

Italy's fiscal and energy challenges are, in practice, a single problem. The government must decide how much of the energy shock to absorb through state support, knowing that each euro of relief spending adds to a debt stock that financial markets already price at a premium over German or French sovereign bonds. A large, open-ended subsidy programme risks triggering renewed scrutiny from European institutions at precisely the moment Rome is seeking their understanding.

For the EU, Italy represents a test case with implications well beyond Rome. If Brussels accepts that defence spending and energy support justify sustained deficit overruns in one of the bloc's largest economies, it will face parallel pressure from other member states in similar positions. Conversely, a strict application of fiscal rules during a period of acute energy stress could harden domestic opposition to EU economic governance across Southern Europe, adding a political dimension to what is formally a technocratic process.

The immediate calendar is set by the EU's assessment of Italy's fiscal plans under its revised Stability and Growth Pact framework, with any formal procedure likely to crystallise in early 2027. Markets will watch the spread between Italian and German ten-year bonds as a real-time indicator of how credibly investors view Rome's fiscal path. For Italian households, the more pressing deadline is the coming heating season, when the full weight of higher energy bills will be felt, and when political patience — already strained — may run shortest.
